source.title: Vision-Language Models Learn Super Images for Efficient Partially Relevant Video Retrieval
source.authors: Taichi Nishimura; Shota Nakada; Masayoshi Kondo

record.tranche_reason: It compares VLM backbone sizes on video-retrieval performance, extending the downstream-performance question to a vision-language video task; it does not test language-model pretraining loss scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al. as motivation but does not reproduce or test their language-model loss or compute-allocation results. Its own backbone-size comparisons measure downstream retrieval performance, bearing on V6. Other results about grid size, adapters, sampling, and reranking are not rows for the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The paper is a video-retrieval method paper (QASIR with super images). It cites Kaplan et al. only to motivate using larger CLIP backbones, then reports its own method's retrieval scores with three off-the-shelf CLIP backbones. Only two model sizes are compared (B/32 vs L/14), and they also differ in patch size and GFLOPs. L14 vs L14-336 differs only in input resolution. No loss or compute sweep and no fitted or predictive relation is reported, so 'predictably with scale' (V6) cannot be assessed. The backbone comparison is a trade-off analysis of the method, not a test of a scaling law in language models.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but the main conclusions are about super images. Off-the-shelf VLMs generalise zero-shot to super images via query attention. Fine-tuned QASIR at 2×2 nearly matches 1×1 at lower cost. Hybrid high/low-efficiency QASIR balances cost and performance. Larger VLMs, higher resolution and smaller grids are named as performance–cost trade-off parameters.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares CLIP-based VLM backbones on video-retrieval benchmarks rather than training language models at varied parameter, token, and compute scales and fitting held-out cross-entropy laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Retrieval scores vary with dataset, grid size, image resolution, and whether QASIR is fine-tuned. The fixed-grid rows show higher sumR for larger backbones, but the comparison also changes image resolution for L14-336.

fits_no_version.finding: Within QASIR, swapping CLIP-B/32 for CLIP-L/14 raises retrieval sumR on all three datasets, zero-shot and fine-tuned, at about 18x the image GFLOPs. Examples: ActivityNet 144.4 to 165.6 zero-shot, and 171.4 to 197.9 fine-tuned, at the 1×1 grid.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger pretrained CLIP vision-language backbones give better zero-shot and adapter-tuned partially relevant video retrieval, at higher compute cost (two-point comparison, confounded with patch size).

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says code will be released upon acceptance
record.peer_reviewed: ACM Trans. Multim. Comput. Commun. Appl.
record.problems: The backbone comparison contains only three configurations; L14 and L14-336 have nearly the same parameter count but differ in image resolution. No uncertainty estimates or scaling-law fit are reported, and retrieval results cannot establish a predictive power law.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 2 and 3 also report results for 2×2 through 6×6 grids. Those grid-size conditions are not extracted here; rows are restricted to the 1×1 setting to give a fixed-grid comparison of backbone sizes. Other recall metrics in the same rows are omitted because sumR is the paper's reported overall comparison metric.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss measured or swept over parameters, tokens or compute.
No fits on small runs and no extrapolation.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
No power-law fit in vision or video; no model is trained at varied scale.
Only two off-the-shelf CLIP sizes are used, confounded with patch size. No predictive relation with scale or loss is tested.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 'supports' label is removed. Scale enters only as a two-backbone design choice (B/32 vs L/14) that also changes patch size, and L14-336 differs from L14 only in resolution. No scaling relation is measured, so the study is classed as T4 and the directional finding goes under fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out language-model pretraining cross-entropy sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No fits from smaller language-model runs or predictions of larger-run loss.
No fixed-compute language-model training allocation between parameters and tokens.
No architecture-depth or width comparison at fixed parameter count for language-model loss.
The study evaluates video retrieval, but does not test whether a power-law form holds across modalities or training regimes.
Tests retrieval performance across a few VLM backbones, not a fitted predictive relationship with pretraining loss or a power-law curve; other downstream tasks are not tested.
No analysis of language-model scaling-law fitting choices, exponents, or curve bending.

rows.subject: QASIR-L14
rows.operation_detail: Compared QASIR retrieval performance across VLM backbones; fixed at 1×1 grid.
rows.note: The larger backbone has higher sumR than QASIR-B32.
rows.check: Single two-point comparison of CLIP-B/32 vs CLIP-L/14 within the authors' method. The backbones also differ in patch size (32 vs 14) and image GFLOPs (8.8 vs 162), so this is not a scale-predictability measure. Parameter counts include the text encoder.

rows.note: This configuration also uses higher image resolution than the B32 reference.
rows.check: L14-336 has the same parameter count as L14 (427.9 vs 427.6 M); only input resolution differs. Against B32 it also changes patch size and resolution. Not a model-scale comparison.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: 1×1 QASIR retrieval on ActivityNet Captions, TVR, and Charades-STA, in zero-shot and fine-tuned settings
reader_labels.reason: At the reported 1×1 setting, sumR is higher for the larger L14 and L14-336 backbones than for B32 on all three datasets in both settings (r2–r3, r5–r6, r8–r9, r11–r12, r14–r15, r17–r18). This is directional downstream evidence, not a fitted prediction law.
